front: Crushing chest pain, and the tracing shows ST elevation in two neighboring leads. The first troponin has not come back.
bottom: Reperfuse. Do not wait for the troponin.

bullets.clue: Contiguous ST elevation is already the decision. Troponin can still be normal in the first hour.
bullets.treat: Give aspirin unless it is unsafe, and activate the reperfusion path.
bullets.trap: Holding the patient in the emergency department for a second biomarker.

source.recommendation: ST elevation in two contiguous leads is a reperfusion diagnosis. Biomarkers confirm injury later. They do not delay the first hour.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Reperfuse. Do not wait for the troponin.

front: A patient in atrial fibrillation is hypotensive, cold, and having ischemic pain. The rate is very fast.

bullets.clue: Instability means hypotension, ischemia, or pulmonary edema, not a number on the monitor alone.
bullets.treat: Synchronized cardioversion is the immediate move. Rate-control pills are for the stable patient.
bullets.trap: Starting a beta blocker and rechecking in an hour while the pressure is falling.

source.recommendation: Unstable atrial fibrillation is an electrical problem first. The 2023 guideline keeps cardioversion for instability.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Cardiovert. This rhythm is unstable.

front: Sudden tearing pain to the back, a missing pulse on one side, and a wide mediastinum. The tracing has no ST elevation.
bottom: Control the heart rate, then the pressure, and repair an ascending tear.

bullets.clue: A beta blocker comes before a pure vasodilator so the heart does not race against a falling pressure.
bullets.treat: Ascending aorta involvement is a surgical emergency. Do not give a clot-busting drug for the pain.
bullets.trap: Treating the pain as a clot and thrombolysing a dissection.

source.recommendation: Acute aortic syndrome is a pulse deficit and a mediastinum, not an ST-elevation equivalent. Rate control precedes vasodilation.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Control the heart rate, then the pressure, and repair an ascending tear.

front: Chest pain is better sitting and leaning forward. The tracing has ST elevation in many leads and depression of the PR segment.
bottom: This is pericardial inflammation, not an occluded artery.

bullets.clue: The pain is positional. The ST elevation is widespread, and the PR segment is depressed.
bullets.treat: An anti-inflammatory plus colchicine is the usual first plan when the story fits and the coronaries are not the question.
bullets.trap: Sending a clot-busting drug for widespread ST elevation.

source.recommendation: Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression and positional pain is pericarditis. Colchicine reduces recurrence.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is pericardial inflammation, not an occluded artery.

front: A patient with a soft innocent murmur is scheduled for a dental cleaning and asks for an antibiotic.
bottom: Most murmurs do not get prophylaxis.

bullets.clue: Prophylaxis is for the highest-risk hearts: a prosthetic valve, a prior infection of the valve, certain congenital repairs, and a transplant heart with valvulopathy.
bullets.treat: Use it only for dental work that breaks gum or the tooth root in those patients. Ordinary gastrointestinal procedures do not qualify.
bullets.trap: Prescribing a dental antibiotic for every click or murmur.

source.recommendation: The AHA limited prophylaxis to the highest-risk cardiac conditions and to procedures that manipulate gingival tissue.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Most murmurs do not get prophylaxis.

front: Calf pain comes on with walking and stops with rest. The foot is warm and intact. The ankle pressure is lower than the arm pressure.
bottom: Treat the risk and walk, before you stent a stable leg.

bullets.clue: A low ankle-brachial index confirms the limited blood flow. The skin is not threatened.
bullets.treat: Stop smoking, start a statin and an antiplatelet, and use a supervised walking program.
bullets.trap: Stenting lifestyle-limiting claudication before risk-factor care and exercise.

source.guideline: ACC/AHA lower extremity peripheral artery disease guideline
source.recommendation: Stable claudication is a medical and exercise disease first. Revascularization is for failure of that care or for a threatened limb.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Treat the risk and walk, before you stent a stable leg.

front: Blood pressure is 210 over 120. The patient has a headache but a normal exam, a normal creatinine, a normal tracing, and no chest pain.
bottom: This is severe hypertension without acute organ injury.

bullets.clue: Emergency means acute damage: brain, heart, aorta, kidney, or eye ischemia. A number alone is not that.
bullets.treat: Lower the pressure over hours to days with oral medicine and follow-up. Do not drop it in the parking lot.
bullets.trap: Intravenous drips and a same-hour normalization because the number looks frightening.

source.recommendation: Hypertensive emergency is defined by acute target-organ injury. Severe pressure without injury is not treated with an immediate intravenous drop.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is severe hypertension without acute organ injury.

front: An older adult has exertional syncope, chest tightness, and a slow weak carotid upstroke. The valve area is critically small.
bottom: Replace the valve. Medicine will not fix the opening.

bullets.clue: Syncope, angina, or heart-failure symptoms with severe stenosis mark a short horizon if the valve is left alone.
bullets.treat: Refer for replacement or a transcatheter valve. Blood pressure pills do not open the orifice.
bullets.trap: Watching a symptomatic severe stenosis for another year of medical therapy.

source.recommendation: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis is a valve problem. Afterload reduction does not replace opening the valve.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Replace the valve. Medicine will not fix the opening.

front: A patient who usually retains carbon dioxide is drowsy after an hour on a non-rebreather mask. The oxygen saturation is 100 percent.
bottom: Turn the oxygen down and support the ventilation.

bullets.clue: The drive and the ventilation-perfusion match both change when a retainer is flooded with oxygen.
bullets.treat: Aim the saturation near 88 to 92 percent and use noninvasive ventilation if carbon dioxide and pH are failing.
bullets.trap: Leaving the mask on because the saturation looks perfect.

source.recommendation: Oxygen for a chronic retainer is titrated, not maximized. A normal saturation with a rising carbon dioxide is harm.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Turn the oxygen down and support the ventilation.

front: A well-appearing adult has a fever, a focal infiltrate, and a normal blood pressure, mental status, and respiratory rate. Age is under 65 and there is no confusion or high urea.

bullets.clue: A low CURB-65 or a low-risk severity class supports outpatient care.
bullets.treat: Oral antibiotics and follow-up. Admission is for higher scores, hypoxia, or a social situation that cannot support care.
bullets.trap: Admitting every infiltrate.

source.recommendation: Site of care follows severity, not the mere presence of an infiltrate. Low-risk patients are treated as outpatients.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Treat this pneumonia at home.

front: Weeks of cough, night sweats, and a cavity in an upper lobe. The sputum stain is not back.

bullets.clue: The picture is enough to protect the next patient. The stain confirms later.
bullets.treat: Airborne room, mask, and a public-health report. Do not wait on a negative rapid test to start isolation.
bullets.trap: Leaving the patient in an open bay until the laboratory calls.

source.recommendation: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is isolated on clinical grounds. Confirmation does not come before the mask.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Isolate for airborne spread now.

front: A tall thin young adult has sudden pleuritic pain and a small rim of air on the film. Speech is full sentences and the pressure is normal.
bottom: Watch a small, stable primary pneumothorax.

bullets.clue: Oxygen speeds resorption. A large or breathless pneumothorax needs a drain.
bullets.treat: Observation is for the small stable leak. A shifting trachea and shock is a different emergency.
bullets.trap: Putting a chest tube in every visible line of air.

source.guideline: British Thoracic Society pleural disease guideline
source.recommendation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax that is small and stable can be observed. Size and physiology decide the drain.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Watch a small, stable primary pneumothorax.

front: Pleural fluid protein is more than half the serum protein, and the fluid LDH is more than three-fifths of the serum LDH.

bullets.clue: An exudate means local pleural disease: infection, cancer, clot, or inflammation. A transudate means pressure or protein failure.
bullets.treat: Look in the chest for the cause of an exudate. Do not stop at a diuretic for heart failure when the criteria say exudate.
bullets.trap: Calling every effusion heart failure.

source.guideline: Light criteria, as used in ATS pleural guidance
source.recommendation: Light criteria separate exudate from transudate. Protein ratio above 0.5, LDH ratio above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two-thirds the serum upper limit.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. The fluid is an exudate.

front: Fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, and jaundice. The pressure is falling.
bottom: Drain the bile duct. Antibiotics alone will not empty it.

bullets.clue: The triad is cholangitis. Shock or confusion means the severe form.
bullets.treat: Blood cultures, broad antibiotics, and urgent biliary decompression.
bullets.trap: Admitting for antibiotics and planning a clinic endoscopy next week.

source.recommendation: Obstructive cholangitis needs source control of the duct, not antibiotics alone.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Drain the bile duct. Antibiotics alone will not empty it.

front: Severe abdominal pain and a soft belly in a patient with atrial fibrillation. Lactate is rising.
bottom: The bowel may be ischemic. Image the vessels.

bullets.clue: Pain out of proportion to the exam is the clue. Peritonitis is late.
bullets.treat: CT angiography and surgical or endovascular rescue. Do not wait for guarding.
bullets.trap: Reassuring a soft abdomen and sending the patient home.

source.guideline: ACG and vascular surgical guidance on mesenteric ischemia
source.recommendation: Acute mesenteric ischemia presents before the belly becomes rigid. Lactate and atrial fibrillation raise the stakes.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. The bowel may be ischemic. Image the vessels.

front: Epigastric pain boring to the back, with lipase several times normal. The patient is not in shock and the diagnosis is not in doubt.
bottom: Do not order a CT to prove what the lipase already showed.

bullets.clue: Early feeding as pain allows is better than days of nothing by mouth. Fluids are given, not drowned.
bullets.treat: Save imaging for diagnostic doubt, deterioration, or a later complication.
bullets.trap: Routine admission CT and a week of fasting.

source.recommendation: Lipase and the story diagnose uncomplicated pancreatitis. CT is for uncertainty or complications, and feeding starts early.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Do not order a CT to prove what the lipase already showed.

front: More than six bloody stools a day, a fast heart, and a known history of continuous colonic inflammation from the rectum up.
bottom: This severe flare needs the hospital, not a bigger outpatient dose.

bullets.clue: Exclude Clostridioides and cytomegalovirus before you blame the disease alone. Watch for a widening colon.
bullets.treat: Intravenous steroid, stool studies, and a surgical conversation if the colon dilates or the patient does not turn.
bullets.trap: Adding an outpatient mesalamine and reviewing in a week.

source.recommendation: Severe ulcerative colitis is an inpatient disease. Infection must be excluded, and toxic dilation is a surgical problem.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This severe flare needs the hospital, not a bigger outpatient dose.

front: A pregnant patient has a very high hepatitis B viral load in the third trimester. The infant is not yet born.
bottom: Lower the mother's virus before delivery, and protect the infant at birth.

bullets.clue: Antiviral therapy late in pregnancy cuts transmission when the load is high.
bullets.treat: The newborn still needs vaccine and immunoglobulin. The maternal medicine does not replace that.
bullets.trap: Waiting until delivery and treating only the infant.

source.recommendation: A high third-trimester viral load is treated to reduce perinatal transmission, and the infant still receives active and passive immunization.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Lower the mother's virus before delivery, and protect the infant at birth.

front: A patient with known ascites has fever and a tender belly. The fluid has more than 250 neutrophils per microliter. The culture is pending.

bullets.clue: The neutrophil count is the decision. Culture is often still negative when you must start.
bullets.treat: Antibiotics immediately, and albumin for the patients at highest kidney risk. Look for a cause such as a variceal bleed.
bullets.trap: Waiting overnight for the culture before the first dose.

source.guideline: AASLD ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis guidance
source.recommendation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed at 250 neutrophils and treated before culture returns.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Treat infected ascites now.

front: Potassium is 7 with a wide QRS, and a dose of insulin and calcium has not held. Another patient is drowning in pulmonary edema that diuretics will not move.
bottom: Dialyze for the complication, not for a creatinine target.

bullets.clue: Acid that will not clear, a toxic alcohol, uremic pericarditis, refractory potassium, and refractory fluid are the triggers.
bullets.treat: Call renal replacement for those threats. A stable high creatinine can wait.
bullets.trap: Dialyzing every doubled creatinine in a patient who is making urine and breathing easily.

source.recommendation: Urgent dialysis follows complications: refractory hyperkalemia, overload, acidosis, certain toxins, and uremic emergencies.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Dialyze for the complication, not for a creatinine target.

front: Heavy protein loss from membranous disease, an albumin that is very low, then sudden flank pain and blood in the urine.
bottom: The renal vein may have clotted.

bullets.clue: Nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous, is a clotting state. The pain is the clot, not a new stone by default.
bullets.treat: Image the vein and anticoagulate a clot. Prevent further dehydration.
bullets.trap: Treating the pain as a ureteral stone and forgetting the protein loss.

source.recommendation: Membranous nephropathy with severe hypoalbuminemia predisposes to renal vein thrombosis.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. The renal vein may have clotted.

front: Creatinine is up. Urine sodium is under 20, osmolality is high, and the sediment is bland. The patient has been vomiting for two days.
bottom: The kidney is thirsty, not dead.

bullets.clue: A low fraction of excreted sodium and concentrated urine mean the tubules are working and holding salt.
bullets.treat: Give volume and stop the offense. Muddy casts and a urine sodium over 40 point at tubular injury instead.
bullets.trap: Starting dialysis for a dry patient with a bland sediment.

source.recommendation: A low urine sodium and high osmolality with a bland sediment is prerenal physiology. Tubular injury wastes sodium.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. The kidney is thirsty, not dead.

front: Fever, a white count, and an obstructing ureteral stone on the scan. The patient is vomiting.
bottom: Decompress the kidney. Do not trial passage.

bullets.clue: Infection behind an obstruction is a closed space. Antibiotics cannot drain it.
bullets.treat: Urgent stent or nephrostomy, plus antibiotics. A comfortable patient with a small sterile stone is the one who may pass it.
bullets.trap: Sending an infected obstructed kidney home with a strainer.

source.recommendation: An obstructing stone plus infection is a drainage emergency. Passage is for the sterile, stable stone.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Decompress the kidney. Do not trial passage.

front: A stable patient needs a contrast study that would change management tonight. The creatinine is only mildly above the old baseline.
bottom: Do the study. Do not cancel a needed answer for a modest creatinine.

bullets.clue: Risk is reduced with volume in the patients who need it. The diagnosis can be more dangerous than the dye.
bullets.treat: Proceed when the result matters. A purely elective study in severe kidney failure is a different conversation.
bullets.trap: Refusing every contrast study once the creatinine is not perfect.

source.recommendation: Needed iodinated contrast is not withheld for mild, stable kidney disease. The clinical question outweighs a small risk.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Do the study. Do not cancel a needed answer for a modest creatinine.

front: Glucose is 480, bicarbonate is 10, and the patient is breathing deeply. Potassium on arrival is 3.0.
bottom: Replace potassium before you start insulin.

bullets.clue: Insulin will drive potassium into cells and can stop the heart if you start from 3.0.
bullets.treat: Fluids first, potassium repletion, then insulin once potassium is safe. Find the trigger.
bullets.trap: A bolus of insulin while the potassium is still 3.0.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: In diabetic ketoacidosis, insulin is held when potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L until potassium is replaced.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Replace potassium before you start insulin.

front: Fever, agitation, and a fast irregular heart in a patient who stopped a thionamide. The gland is not the only organ in trouble.
bottom: Block hormone release, but not with iodine first.

bullets.clue: A beta blocker protects the heart. A thionamide blocks new hormone. Iodine comes after, so the gland is not fueled.
bullets.treat: Give a steroid as well. Do not lead with iodine.
bullets.trap: Iodine on arrival, before the thionamide.

source.recommendation: Thyroid storm treatment is a beta blocker, a thionamide, then iodine, plus a glucocorticoid. Iodine first can load the gland.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Block hormone release, but not with iodine first.

front: An older adult is hypothermic and slow, with a puffy face, a low sodium, and a high TSH. A trigger infection is present.
bottom: Give thyroid hormone and cover the adrenal until you know it is safe.

bullets.clue: Severe hypothyroidism can hide adrenal failure. Warming alone does not replace hormone.
bullets.treat: Intravenous thyroid hormone and stress-dose steroid, plus the trigger. Avoid aggressive external heat.
bullets.trap: Warming blankets as the only treatment.

source.recommendation: Myxedema crisis is treated with intravenous thyroid hormone and empiric glucocorticoid until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Give thyroid hormone and cover the adrenal until you know it is safe.

front: Calcium is 14, the patient is confused, and the QT is short. The jugular vein is flat.
bottom: Salt water first, then a drug that will hold the calcium down.

bullets.clue: Volume restores excretion. Calcitonin is a bridge. A bisphosphonate lasts longer.
bullets.treat: Isotonic saline, then the longer-acting drug. Find the cause after the number is moving.
bullets.trap: A loop diuretic in a dry patient as the first order.

source.recommendation: Severe hypercalcemia starts with intravenous saline. A loop diuretic is not the first move in a volume-depleted patient.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Salt water first, then a drug that will hold the calcium down.

front: A woman has missed periods and galactorrhea. Prolactin is several hundred. Vision is intact. MRI shows a pituitary mass.
bottom: A dopamine agonist is first, even for many large tumors.

bullets.clue: Very high prolactin means the mass is making it. A mild rise can be stalk effect from a nonfunctioning mass.
bullets.treat: Cabergoline or bromocriptine, and vision checks. Surgery is for threat to vision or failure of the drug.
bullets.trap: Sending every pituitary mass to surgery the week it is found.

source.recommendation: Prolactinomas are treated first with a dopamine agonist unless vision is acutely threatened or the drug fails.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. A dopamine agonist is first, even for many large tumors.

front: After a vomiting illness the patient is hypotensive, potassium is high, and sodium is low. A cosyntropin test has been ordered but not drawn.
bottom: Give the steroid. Do not wait for the test.

bullets.clue: The picture is adrenal crisis until proven otherwise. The test can be drawn just before the dose if it does not delay care.
bullets.treat: Intravenous glucocorticoid and saline. Look for the trigger.
bullets.trap: Holding hydrocortisone until the stimulation result posts tomorrow.

source.recommendation: Suspected adrenal crisis is treated immediately. Diagnostic testing must not delay the steroid.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Give the steroid. Do not wait for the test.

front: A pregnant patient has bacteria in the urine and no symptoms. A nonpregnant healthy woman has the same culture and feels well.
bottom: Treat the pregnancy. Do not treat the other patient.

bullets.clue: Asymptomatic bacteriuria matters in pregnancy and before some urologic procedures. It does not matter in a well nonpregnant adult.
bullets.treat: A short antibiotic course in pregnancy. No antibiotic for the well nonpregnant adult.
bullets.trap: Treating every positive culture.

source.recommendation: Screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy. Do not treat it in nonpregnant adults without a urologic indication.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Treat the pregnancy. Do not treat the other patient.

front: A positive interferon-gamma release assay, a normal chest film, and no cough, fever, or sweats.
bottom: Treat latent infection. Do not start four drugs.

bullets.clue: The film and the symptoms separate latent infection from disease.
bullets.treat: A latent regimen, and public-health follow-up. Four drugs are for active disease.
bullets.trap: Nine months of four-drug therapy because the blood test was positive.

source.recommendation: A positive release assay with a normal film and no symptoms is latent tuberculosis, treated with a latent regimen.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Treat latent infection. Do not start four drugs.

front: Fever, a rash, and a sore throat two weeks after a new sexual exposure. The antibody test is negative.
bottom: This can still be acute HIV. Order the virus itself.

bullets.clue: Antibody tests miss the window. RNA or an antigen test does not.
bullets.treat: Counsel, confirm with nucleic acid, and link to treatment. Do not clear the patient on a negative antibody.
bullets.trap: Telling the patient the negative antibody ends the question.

source.recommendation: Acute HIV is a viral-load diagnosis. Antibody-only tests are negative in the window.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This can still be acute HIV. Order the virus itself.

front: A red, warm, fluctuant, and exquisitely tender lump on the thigh. The center is pointing.
bottom: Drain it. An antibiotic will not empty a collection.

bullets.clue: Cellulitis without a collection is a drug. A collection is a knife or a needle.
bullets.treat: Incise and drain. Add an antibiotic when there is severe disease, immunosuppression, or surrounding cellulitis that needs it.
bullets.trap: Oral antibiotics and a recheck next week for a drainable abscess.

source.guideline: IDSA skin and soft tissue guideline
source.recommendation: A fluctuant abscess is treated by drainage. Antibiotics are adjuncts, not a substitute.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Drain it. An antibiotic will not empty a collection.

front: Watery diarrhea and a positive Clostridioides toxin, in a patient still taking the antibiotic that started it.
bottom: Stop the offending drug and treat with vancomycin by mouth or with fidaxomicin.

bullets.clue: Metronidazole is no longer the preferred first drug for an initial episode.
bullets.treat: Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, and stop the trigger antibiotic when you can.
bullets.trap: Intravenous metronidazole as the only agent for a routine first episode.

source.recommendation: Initial C. difficile infection is treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, and the inciting antibiotic is stopped.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Stop the offending drug and treat with vancomycin by mouth or with fidaxomicin.

front: A tick from an endemic county was attached for two days and was removed this morning. There is no rash.
bottom: One dose of doxycycline is enough, and only because the rules are met.

bullets.clue: Prophylaxis needs the right tick, enough attachment time, a high local rate, and a start within 72 hours. A tick brushed off in an hour does not qualify.
bullets.treat: A single doxycycline dose when every condition is met. Otherwise watch the skin.
bullets.trap: Three weeks of doxycycline for every tick bite.

source.recommendation: Lyme prophylaxis is a single dose of doxycycline within 72 hours, and only when attachment, species, and local risk all qualify.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. One dose of doxycycline is enough, and only because the rules are met.

front: A traveler returns with fever, confusion, and a parasite load on the smear. Oral chloroquine is what the clinic has.

bullets.clue: Species and region matter for oral therapy. Severe disease, including confusion or high parasite burden, is not an oral-drug problem.
bullets.treat: Artesunate now, and specialist and public-health help. Do not start with oral chloroquine.
bullets.trap: Sending the patient home with chloroquine because the smear is positive.

source.recommendation: Severe malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate. Oral chloroquine is not the drug for severe disease.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Severe malaria needs intravenous artesunate.

front: A routine swab at 36 weeks grows group B streptococcus. The patient feels well and is not in labor.
bottom: Do not treat the colonization now. Treat in labor.

bullets.clue: Antepartum antibiotics do not reliably clear carriage by the time of birth.
bullets.treat: Intrapartum penicillin if the screen is positive, if a prior infant was infected, or if status is unknown and risk is present.
bullets.trap: A week of oral antibiotics at 36 weeks and a belief that labor will be safe.

source.recommendation: Group B streptococcus colonization is treated during labor, not with antepartum antibiotics aimed at clearing the swab.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Do not treat the colonization now. Treat in labor.

front: A patient is 30 weeks pregnant and had a tetanus booster four years ago, before this pregnancy.
bottom: Give tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine in this pregnancy anyway.

bullets.clue: Each pregnancy gets a dose between 27 and 36 weeks so antibody reaches the infant.
bullets.treat: Vaccinate in the window even if a recent tetanus shot was given for another reason before pregnancy.
bullets.trap: Skipping the dose because a tetanus booster is still in date.

source.recommendation: Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, preferably at 27 to 36 weeks, regardless of the prior tetanus interval.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Give tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine in this pregnancy anyway.

front: An unsensitized Rh-negative patient is at 28 weeks. The antibody screen is negative. There has been no bleeding.
bottom: Give Rh immune globulin now, and again if the baby is Rh positive.

bullets.clue: A negative screen means she has not made her own antibody yet. The globulin prevents that.
bullets.treat: Routine dose at 28 weeks, and a dose after bleeding, procedures, or birth of an Rh-positive infant.
bullets.trap: Waiting until delivery for the only dose.

source.recommendation: Unsensitized Rh-negative patients receive anti-D immune globulin at 28 weeks and after potential fetomaternal hemorrhage.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Give Rh immune globulin now, and again if the baby is Rh positive.

front: A pregnant patient has unilateral pain and a positive pregnancy test. She is hypotensive and the belly is rigid.
bottom: Operate. This is rupture until proven otherwise.

bullets.clue: Methotrexate is only for a stable patient who can return for serial hormone checks and has no rupture.
bullets.treat: Resuscitation and surgery. Do not send a shocky patient for a methotrexate injection.
bullets.trap: Methotrexate in the emergency department for a peritonitic patient.

source.recommendation: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a surgical emergency. Methotrexate is reserved for selected stable patients.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Operate. This is rupture until proven otherwise.

front: A patient at 26 weeks has no diabetes history. The one-hour glucose screen has not been done.

bullets.clue: Earlier screening is for patients with risk. Universal screening is this window.
bullets.treat: Do the glucose screen. Treat gestational diabetes with diet first and insulin when targets are missed.
bullets.trap: Waiting until 36 weeks because the patient feels well.

source.recommendation: Universal gestational diabetes screening is at 24 to 28 weeks. Earlier testing is added for high-risk patients.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Screen now, in the 24-to-28-week window.

front: Two months after delivery a patient has a fast heart and anxiety, then a few weeks later is exhausted with a high TSH. The gland is not tender. Antibodies of Graves disease are absent.
bottom: This is a postpartum leak of stored hormone, not a gland that needs to be blocked.

bullets.clue: The toxic phase is release of preformed hormone. Antithyroid drugs do not stop a leak.
bullets.treat: A beta blocker if the toxic phase bothers her, then watch for the low phase, which may need replacement.
bullets.trap: Starting methimazole for a self-limited thyroiditis.

source.recommendation: Postpartum thyroiditis is a destructive leak followed by hypothyroidism. The toxic phase is not treated with a thionamide.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. This is a postpartum leak of stored hormone, not a gland that needs to be blocked.

front: A toddler has waves of screaming and drawing up the legs, then calm periods. Later there is dark red mucus in the stool. Ultrasound shows a target.
bottom: The bowel has telescoped. Reduce it with air if the belly is not peritonitic.

bullets.clue: Currant-jelly stool is late. The waves of pain are earlier.
bullets.treat: Air or contrast enema when there is no perforation. Surgery if the belly is peritonitic or reduction fails.
bullets.trap: A laxative and a next-day clinic visit.

source.guideline: AAP and pediatric surgical standard for intussusception
source.recommendation: Ileocolic intussusception in a stable child is reduced with an air enema. Peritonitis or perforation goes to the operating room.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. The bowel has telescoped. Reduce it with air if the belly is not peritonitic.

front: A newborn hip clunks on the Ortolani maneuver. The family asks for an x-ray today.
bottom: Ultrasound, not a plain film, at this age.

bullets.clue: The femoral head is cartilage. A film is useful later, when bone has formed.
bullets.treat: Refer and image with ultrasound. A Pavlik harness is the usual first treatment when the hip is unstable.
bullets.trap: A frog-leg x-ray in the nursery as the deciding test.

source.guideline: AAP developmental dysplasia of the hip guidance
source.recommendation: Neonatal hip instability is evaluated with ultrasound. Radiographs become useful after the femoral head ossifies.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Ultrasound, not a plain film, at this age.

front: An infant has a weak cry, constipation, and descending weakness. The family has been dipping the pacifier in honey.
bottom: This is botulism from ingested spores, not a stroke.

bullets.clue: Honey is a classic exposure under one year. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release.
bullets.treat: Support the airway and get botulism antitoxin through public health. Do not wait for a stool result to protect the breathing.
bullets.trap: A course of antibiotics as the main treatment.

source.recommendation: Infant botulism follows honey or soil exposure. Airway support and antitoxin matter more than the confirmatory stool test.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is botulism from ingested spores, not a stroke.

front: A comfortable three-year-old has one red eardrum, a low fever, and a parent who can return tomorrow. Pain is mild.
bottom: You may watch this ear rather than start an antibiotic today.

bullets.clue: Age under six months, a severe picture, or otorrhea is not an observation case.
bullets.treat: Pain control and a firm follow-up. Treat if the child is an infant, looks ill, or cannot be rechecked.
bullets.trap: Observation for a two-month-old.

source.recommendation: Observation is an option for selected older children with mild unilateral acute otitis media when follow-up is certain.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. You may watch this ear rather than start an antibiotic today.

front: A fingerstick lead level is high. The child looks well. A parent asks about chelation today.
bottom: Confirm with a venous sample before you chelate.

bullets.clue: Capillary tests are contaminated easily. Venous blood is the decision.
bullets.treat: Confirm, remove the exposure, and chelate only at the venous thresholds that call for it.
bullets.trap: Chelating a fingerstick result the same day.

source.recommendation: An elevated capillary lead level is confirmed with venous blood before chelation.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Confirm with a venous sample before you chelate.

front: A patient suddenly cannot speak or lift an arm. The last moment anyone knows they were well was 90 minutes ago. The head CT shows no blood.
bottom: This is a reperfusion decision. Do not wait for an MRI.

bullets.clue: A noncontrast CT excludes hemorrhage. MRI is better for ischemia and too slow to lead.
bullets.treat: Treat within the time and imaging rules, and involve stroke neurology. Glucose and the story still matter.
bullets.trap: Waiting for diffusion MRI before calling the stroke team.

source.recommendation: Disabling stroke with a known last-well time and a CT without hemorrhage is evaluated for reperfusion immediately.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is a reperfusion decision. Do not wait for an MRI.

front: A first seizure happened while the sodium was 118. The sodium is now normal, the exam is normal, and the electroencephalogram is pending.
bottom: Do not commit this patient to years of a seizure drug tonight.

bullets.clue: A provoked seizure is treated by fixing the provocation. Recurrence risk is not the same as an unprovoked seizure.
bullets.treat: Correct the sodium, look for other triggers, and decide on a drug only if the workup shows an ongoing epileptic tendency.
bullets.trap: Loading a lifelong antiseizure drug for a sodium of 118.

source.recommendation: A clearly provoked seizure is managed by removing the provocation. Long-term medication is not automatic.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Do not commit this patient to years of a seizure drug tonight.

front: A 74-year-old has a new headache, scalp tenderness, and pain in the jaw while chewing. One eye has just dimmed.
bottom: Start a steroid now. Do not wait for the biopsy.

bullets.clue: Vision loss in giant cell arteritis is a same-hour problem. The sedimentation rate supports the story and must not delay treatment.
bullets.treat: High-dose glucocorticoid, then a prompt temporal-artery biopsy. The biopsy can still be read after the first doses.
bullets.trap: Scheduling a biopsy next week and withholding steroid until then.

source.recommendation: Suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms is treated with immediate glucocorticoid. Biopsy follows and is not a reason to wait.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Start a steroid now. Do not wait for the biopsy.

front: The worst headache of a patient's life peaks in one second. The exam is now normal. CT was not done.
bottom: Image before anyone says this is a migraine.

bullets.clue: A thunderclap headache is subarachnoid blood until the workup says otherwise.
bullets.treat: Noncontrast CT now. If the CT is negative and the story remains classic, the spinal fluid is next.
bullets.trap: A triptan and discharge without imaging.

source.recommendation: Thunderclap headache is imaged immediately. A negative CT does not end a classic story. Lumbar puncture is the next step.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Image before anyone says this is a migraine.

front: A patient has been shaking for six minutes and is still shaking. A home drug level has been ordered.
bottom: Give a benzodiazepine now. Do not wait for the level.

bullets.clue: Five minutes of seizure is status. The level can be drawn, but it does not lead.
bullets.treat: Benzodiazepine, then a longer-acting antiseizure drug, then airway support. Look for glucose and other triggers.
bullets.trap: Waiting for the phenytoin level before the first dose.

source.guideline: Neurocritical Care Society status epilepticus guideline
source.recommendation: Ongoing seizure activity is treated immediately with a benzodiazepine. Drug levels do not delay the first dose.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Give a benzodiazepine now. Do not wait for the level.

front: Two days after the last drink: tremor, a fast heart, and sweating. The patient then has a seizure.
bottom: This is withdrawal. A benzodiazepine treats it.

bullets.clue: Alcohol withdrawal seizures are not epilepsy. An antipsychotic does not replace the GABA drug.
bullets.treat: Benzodiazepines, thiamine, and a monitored setting. Phenobarbital is an alternative protocol, not an antipsychotic.
bullets.trap: Haloperidol as the only drug for a withdrawing patient.

source.recommendation: Alcohol withdrawal, including seizures, is treated with a benzodiazepine. Antipsychotics do not treat the withdrawal state.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is withdrawal. A benzodiazepine treats it.

front: A patient is mute, holds odd postures, and has waxy flexibility. An antipsychotic was recently increased.
bottom: This can be catatonia. A benzodiazepine is the test and the treatment.

bullets.clue: More antipsychotic can worsen catatonia and can hide malignant catatonia.
bullets.treat: Lorazepam challenge and hold the antipsychotic. Look for the medical cause.
bullets.trap: Raising the antipsychotic because the patient looks withdrawn.

source.recommendation: Catatonia is treated with a benzodiazepine, not with a higher antipsychotic dose.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This can be catatonia. A benzodiazepine is the test and the treatment.

front: A teenager with very low weight has a heart rate of 38 overnight, a temperature of 35 degrees, and a potassium of 2.8.
bottom: Admit for medical danger. Outpatient therapy is not the first step.

bullets.clue: Bradycardia, hypothermia, and electrolyte collapse are admission criteria, not motivational problems.
bullets.treat: Monitored refeeding, electrolyte replacement, and then the eating-disorder treatment.
bullets.trap: A therapy referral slip from the emergency department.

source.recommendation: Medical instability in anorexia nervosa is an indication for admission, before outpatient psychotherapy.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Admit for medical danger. Outpatient therapy is not the first step.

front: Ten days after birth a parent cannot sleep even when the infant sleeps, cannot bond, and describes thoughts of harming the infant.
bottom: This is not the baby blues. Treat it as an emergency.

bullets.clue: Blues fade inside two weeks and do not include harm thoughts or loss of function.
bullets.treat: Same-day psychiatric and pediatric safety assessment. Do not send the pair home on reassurance.
bullets.trap: A handout about baby blues and a six-week postpartum visit.

source.recommendation: Postpartum depression with impaired function or infant-harm thoughts is urgent. Baby blues are mild and self-limited.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is not the baby blues. Treat it as an emergency.

front: A hot swollen knee and a fever. No one has put a needle in it. Antibiotics have been ordered.
bottom: Tap the joint before the antibiotic, unless the delay would be dangerous.

bullets.clue: The fluid white count and the culture decide septic arthritis. Antibiotics first can sterilize the only sample.
bullets.treat: Aspirate, then antibiotics, and orthopedic drainage if the joint is septic.
bullets.trap: Three days of antibiotics with no synovial fluid.

source.guideline: IDSA and orthopedic standard for septic arthritis
source.recommendation: A suspected septic joint is aspirated before antibiotics when that does not meaningfully delay treatment.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Tap the joint before the antibiotic, unless the delay would be dangerous.

front: A leg bone is through the skin after a crash. Pulses are present. Tetanus status is unknown.
bottom: Antibiotics, tetanus protection, and the operating room. Not a clinic splint.

bullets.clue: An open fracture is contaminated. Time to irrigation matters.
bullets.treat: Intravenous antibiotic, tetanus update, and urgent debridement.
bullets.trap: A sugar-tong splint and orthopedic clinic next week.

source.recommendation: Open fractures need immediate antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, and urgent operative irrigation.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Antibiotics, tetanus protection, and the operating room. Not a clinic splint.

front: After a tibial fracture the calf is wooden and the pain spikes when the toes are stretched. The foot still has a pulse.
bottom: This is a compartment syndrome. A pulse does not clear it.

bullets.clue: Pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment come before pulselessness, which is late.
bullets.treat: Measure the pressure if the exam is uncertain, or go straight to fasciotomy when the exam is clear.
bullets.trap: Reassurance because the dorsalis pedis is palpable.

source.guideline: Orthopedic trauma standard for compartment syndrome
source.recommendation: Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis. Palpable pulses do not exclude it.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is a compartment syndrome. A pulse does not clear it.

front: Low back pain, numbness in the saddle, and a bladder that will not empty. Both legs are weak.
bottom: Image the cauda equina and decompress it. This is not a therapy referral.

bullets.clue: Urinary retention and saddle anesthesia are the red flags. Unilateral sciatica without them is not this.
bullets.treat: Emergency MRI and surgical decompression.
bullets.trap: Ibuprofen and physical therapy next month.

source.recommendation: Cauda equina syndrome with retention or saddle anesthesia is an emergency MRI and decompression.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Image the cauda equina and decompress it. This is not a therapy referral.

front: Platelets are 12,000, hemoglobin is falling, the smear shows broken red cells, and the patient is confused. Coagulation times are normal.
bottom: This is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Exchange the plasma.

bullets.clue: Normal coagulation times separate it from disseminated intravascular coagulation. Platelets will be consumed.
bullets.treat: Plasma exchange and the disease-specific therapy. Do not transfuse platelets for the number alone.
bullets.trap: A platelet transfusion to make the count look better.

source.recommendation: TTP is microangiopathic hemolysis and thrombocytopenia with relatively normal coagulation. Platelet transfusion can worsen thrombosis.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Exchange the plasma.

front: A well child has bruises and a platelet count of 20,000 a week after a viral illness. Hemoglobin and white cells are normal. There is no wet bleeding.
bottom: Watch. Do not transfuse platelets for the number.

bullets.clue: Typical immune thrombocytopenia after a virus in a well child often recovers.
bullets.treat: Observation when there is no significant bleeding. Treat bleeding, not the integer.
bullets.trap: A platelet transfusion and a bone marrow biopsy the same day in a well child.

source.recommendation: Children with newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia and no or mild bleeding are observed.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Watch. Do not transfuse platelets for the number.

front: A patient with atrial fibrillation and a remote stroke risk, on a blood thinner, needs a tooth extracted. Kidney function is normal and the stroke was three years ago.

bullets.clue: Bridging adds bleeding. It is for the rare very high thrombotic risk, such as a mechanical mitral valve or a very recent clot.
bullets.treat: Hold the thinner for the shortest safe window and restart. No low-molecular-weight heparin in the gap for ordinary atrial fibrillation.
bullets.trap: A heparin bridge for every patient who misses a dose of warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant.

source.recommendation: Most patients with atrial fibrillation should not receive heparin bridging around a procedure. Bridging increases major bleeding.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Do not bridge with heparin.

front: Platelets fall by half on day 7 of heparin, and a leg is swollen. Yesterday's count was normal on day 2.
bottom: Stop every heparin and start a different anticoagulant.

bullets.clue: The timing, five to ten days, or sooner on re-exposure, plus thrombosis, is the disease.
bullets.treat: A non-heparin anticoagulant. Do not start warfarin alone while the platelet count is still low.
bullets.trap: Holding heparin and waiting with no anticoagulant while a clot is present.

source.recommendation: Suspected HIT means all heparin stops and a non-heparin anticoagulant starts. Warfarin monotherapy in the acute phase is harmful.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Stop every heparin and start a different anticoagulant.

front: A painful rash with skin that shears off, plus mouth and eye erosions, starting two weeks after a new seizure drug.
bottom: Stop the drug. This is a severe cutaneous reaction.

bullets.clue: One to three weeks after the drug is the usual window. Mucosa separates this from a simple morbilliform rash.
bullets.treat: Stop the culprit, supportive care as for a burn, and do not restart the drug. A short steroid burst is not a reason to continue it.
bullets.trap: Diphenhydramine and one more week of the same drug.

source.guideline: AAD guidance on severe cutaneous drug reactions
source.recommendation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are drug emergencies. The culprit stops immediately.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Stop the drug. This is a severe cutaneous reaction.

front: Limb pain far beyond the redness, bullae, and a patient who is becoming toxic over a few hours.
bottom: This is a necrotizing infection. The treatment is the operating room.

bullets.clue: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae, or crepitus are late enough. Do not wait for crepitus.
bullets.treat: Urgent surgical exploration, broad antibiotics, and resuscitation.
bullets.trap: Another day of intravenous antibiotics and a marked border.

source.recommendation: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection is a surgical diagnosis. Antibiotics without debridement are not sufficient.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. This is a necrotizing infection. The treatment is the operating room.

front: A pigmented lesion on the back has changed color and shape over two months. A clinic offers to freeze it today.
bottom: Excise it so a pathologist can see the depth. Do not destroy it.

bullets.clue: Frozen destruction leaves no specimen and no thickness.
bullets.treat: Full-thickness excisional biopsy with a narrow margin. Depth decides the rest of the operation.
bullets.trap: Cryotherapy of a changing pigmented lesion.

source.recommendation: A suspected melanoma is removed with an excisional biopsy so Breslow thickness can be measured.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Excise it so a pathologist can see the depth. Do not destroy it.

front: A healthy 46-year-old has never been screened for colorectal cancer and has no symptoms.
bottom: Start screening. Forty-five is the age, not fifty.

bullets.clue: Stool testing or a visual exam are both acceptable when the patient will complete one of them.
bullets.treat: Offer a screening test now and repeat on the correct interval. Do not wait for symptoms.
bullets.trap: Reassurance that screening starts at 50.

source.recommendation: The USPSTF recommends colorectal cancer screening from age 45 to 75.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Start screening. Forty-five is the age, not fifty.

front: A 62-year-old smoked a pack a day for 30 years and quit 10 years ago. No symptoms.
bottom: Offer a yearly low-dose chest CT.

bullets.clue: The window is age 50 to 80, at least 20 pack-years, and current smoking or quitting within 15 years.
bullets.treat: Annual low-dose CT while the patient still meets the rule. A chest x-ray is not the screening test.
bullets.trap: A plain film every year, or no screen because the patient already quit.

source.recommendation: Annual low-dose CT is recommended for adults 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year history who smoke or quit within 15 years.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Offer a yearly low-dose chest CT.

front: A 42-year-old woman with average risk has never had a mammogram and feels well.
bottom: Start mammography. The recommended rhythm is every other year.

bullets.clue: The current preventive range for average risk is 40 through 74.
bullets.treat: Biennial screening mammography. Do not promise that a normal film rules out every cancer.
bullets.trap: Waiting until 50 because an older guideline said so.

source.recommendation: The 2024 USPSTF recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 at average risk.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Start mammography. The recommended rhythm is every other year.

front: A 68-year-old man smoked for twenty years and quit at 60. He has no abdominal symptoms.
bottom: One ultrasound of the aorta. He does not need it repeated every year.

bullets.clue: Men 65 to 75 who have ever smoked get a one-time screen. A never-smoker is a different, weaker case.
bullets.treat: One abdominal ultrasound.
bullets.trap: Yearly ultrasounds for life because he once smoked.

source.recommendation: One-time ultrasound screening for abdominal aortic aneurysm is recommended in men 65 to 75 who have ever smoked.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. One ultrasound of the aorta. He does not need it repeated every year.

front: A healthy 68-year-old with no vascular disease asks for a daily aspirin to stay healthy.
bottom: Do not start aspirin for primary prevention at this age.

bullets.clue: Bleeding outweighs the gain for most adults 60 and older who have never had vascular disease.
bullets.treat: Talk about pressure, lipids, and smoking instead. Aspirin for someone who already has vascular disease is a different question.
bullets.trap: A baby aspirin for every older adult.

source.recommendation: The USPSTF recommends against starting aspirin for primary prevention in adults 60 and older.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Do not start aspirin for primary prevention at this age.

front: A 66-year-old woman has never broken a bone and has never had a bone-density test.
bottom: Offer a density test. Sixty-five is the age for women.

bullets.clue: Earlier testing is for risk that equals a 65-year-old, not for every perimenopausal patient.
bullets.treat: DEXA now. Treat based on the score and fracture risk, not on the test alone.
bullets.trap: Waiting until the first fracture.

source.recommendation: The USPSTF recommends osteoporosis screening in women 65 and older. Confirm the statement is still current before the feed is shown to students.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Offer a density test. Sixty-five is the age for women.

front: A friend is unconscious, breathing four times a minute, with pinpoint pupils. A syringe was in the room.
bottom: Give naloxone and breathe for the patient.

bullets.clue: The urine drug screen does not arrive in time and does not reverse the receptor.
bullets.treat: Naloxone, airway support, and a watch period because the drug can outlast the antidote.
bullets.trap: Waiting for a toxicology panel before the antidote.

source.recommendation: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression is treated with naloxone and ventilation immediately.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Give naloxone and breathe for the patient.

front: A patient swallowed a bottle of acetaminophen six hours ago and feels fine. Liver enzymes are still normal.
bottom: Plot the level and start the antidote if it is above the line. Do not wait for the enzymes.

bullets.clue: Injury shows up after the enzymes do. A normal ALT at six hours is expected and useless as reassurance.
bullets.treat: N-acetylcysteine when the treatment line is crossed, the time is unknown, or the history is large.
bullets.trap: Discharge because the liver tests are normal tonight.

source.recommendation: Acetaminophen toxicity is decided with a timed level and the Rumack-Matthew line. Normal early liver enzymes do not clear the patient.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Plot the level and start the antidote if it is above the line. Do not wait for the enzymes.

front: Headache and nausea in a family whose heater has been running. The pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. They look pink.
bottom: The oximeter cannot see this poisoning. Send co-oximetry.

bullets.clue: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and shifts the curve. Standard pulse oximetry stays falsely normal.
bullets.treat: High-flow oxygen, a co-oximeter level, and hyperbaric consideration for severe cases.
bullets.trap: Reassurance from a normal pulse oximeter.

source.recommendation: Carbon monoxide poisoning is diagnosed with co-oximetry. Standard pulse oximetry does not detect it.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. The oximeter cannot see this poisoning. Send co-oximetry.

front: Sudden severe testicular pain, a high-riding testis, and no cremasteric reflex. Onset was one hour ago.
bottom: Go to the operating room. Do not wait on an ultrasound if it will delay the knife.

bullets.clue: The other side is fixed at the same operation. Ultrasound is for the doubtful exam, not for a clear one.
bullets.treat: Immediate urology exploration.
bullets.trap: Scheduled outpatient ultrasound tomorrow.

source.recommendation: A classic torsion exam goes to immediate exploration. Imaging is only allowed if it does not delay surgery.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Go to the operating room. Do not wait on an ultrasound if it will delay the knife.

front: A patient speaks only Spanish. The consent for surgery is about to be done by the patient's eight-year-old child.
bottom: Use a professional interpreter. A child is not the interpreter.

bullets.clue: Family may stay for support. They do not replace a qualified interpreter for consent.
bullets.treat: A professional interpreter, in person or by video, before the signature.
bullets.trap: Letting the child translate the risks to save time.

source.guideline: Joint Commission patient rights on communication
source.recommendation: Informed consent requires a qualified interpreter when you and the patient do not share a language. Children should not interpret.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Use a professional interpreter. A child is not the interpreter.

front: A medication error reached the patient and caused harm. The chart can be written so the error is hard to see.

bullets.clue: Disclosure includes what is known, what it means, and what will be done. Blame of a colleague is not the script.
bullets.treat: An honest conversation, care for the harm, and a report through the safety system.
bullets.trap: Hiding the event in vague chart language.

source.guideline: AMA Code of Medical Ethics on disclosure
source.recommendation: Physicians disclose harmful errors to patients. Concealment is an ethics failure and a safety failure.

diagram.alt: Takeaway. Tell the patient what happened.

front: Fasting glucose is 132 on two mornings.

bullets.clue: A second fasting value confirms it.
bullets.treat: Confirm, then start treatment.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for symptoms.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: ADA diagnoses diabetes at fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, confirmed.

diagram.alt: Threshold. Diabetes starts at 126 mg/dL.

front: A1c is 6.6 percent. There are no symptoms.

bullets.clue: Symptoms are not required.
bullets.treat: Confirm and treat.
bullets.trap: Do not call 6.6 prediabetes.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: A1c of 6.5 percent or higher diagnoses diabetes.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Diabetes starts at 6.5 percent.

front: Fasting glucose is 112 and A1c is 6.0 percent.

bullets.clue: Fasting 100 to 125 is the range.
bullets.treat: Lifestyle, then recheck.
bullets.trap: Do not start insulin.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: Prediabetes is fasting glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL or A1c 5.7 to 6.4 percent.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. This is prediabetes.

front: Glucose is 700, ketones are absent, and the patient is dry.

bullets.clue: This is the hyperosmolar state, not ketoacidosis.
bullets.treat: Saline, then insulin after potassium is known.
bullets.trap: Do not lead with insulin.

source.guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
source.recommendation: Hyperosmolar state is volume first. Insulin follows potassium.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Fluids first.

front: A thyroid nodule is hot and TSH is suppressed.
bottom: A hot nodule is rarely cancer.

bullets.clue: A cold nodule is the one that needs a needle.
bullets.treat: Treat the hot nodule. Biopsy the cold one.
bullets.trap: Do not biopsy every hot nodule.

source.recommendation: Hyperfunctioning nodules are rarely malignant.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. A hot nodule is rarely cancer.

front: A solid thyroid nodule is taller than wide. TSH is normal.

bullets.clue: Shape drives the biopsy when TSH is normal.
bullets.treat: Fine-needle aspiration.
bullets.trap: Do not watch a high-suspicion nodule for a year.

source.recommendation: High-suspicion ultrasound features warrant aspiration.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Needle it.

front: Home pressure averages 138 over 86 on several days.

bullets.clue: Out-of-office readings confirm the number.
bullets.treat: Lifestyle and medicine, then recheck at home.
bullets.trap: Do not treat one rushed office reading.

source.recommendation: Most treated adults are treated to below 130/80 mm Hg.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Treat toward below 130/80.

front: A patient with a prior heart attack is on no statin.

bullets.clue: The expected LDL drop is about half.
bullets.treat: Atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg.
bullets.trap: Do not start a low dose by habit.

source.recommendation: Clinical atherosclerotic disease gets a high-intensity statin.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Use a high-intensity statin.

front: Atrial fibrillation and a mechanical mitral valve.
bottom: Warfarin, not a direct oral drug.

bullets.clue: Mechanical valves stay on warfarin.
bullets.treat: Warfarin, with a bridge when it is held.
bullets.trap: Do not use apixaban.

source.recommendation: DOACs are avoided in mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Warfarin, not a direct oral drug.

front: New heart failure with a low ejection fraction. The patient is already on a water pill.

bullets.clue: The water pill only treats congestion.
bullets.treat: Beta blocker, ARNI or ACE, mineralocorticoid antagonist, then an SGLT2 inhibitor.
bullets.trap: Do not discharge on a diuretic only.

source.recommendation: HFrEF therapy is those four disease-modifying classes.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Add the four disease drugs.

front: Rest pain, ST depression, and a rising troponin. No ST elevation.

bullets.clue: A rising troponin is injury without ST elevation.
bullets.treat: Antithrombotic therapy and an early invasive plan.
bullets.trap: Do not call it reflux.

source.recommendation: Non-ST-elevation ACS with a rising troponin is not discharged.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Do not send this home.

front: No pulse and a wide irregular rhythm.

bullets.clue: Drugs do not come before the shock.
bullets.treat: Defibrillate, then resume compressions.
bullets.trap: Do not delay the shock.

source.recommendation: Pulseless ventricular fibrillation is defibrillated immediately.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Shock first.

front: Pressure is falling from a large lung clot.

bullets.clue: Heparin alone is not enough when there is shock.
bullets.treat: Thrombolysis or embolectomy, then heparin.
bullets.trap: Do not send the patient to the ward.

source.recommendation: High-risk pulmonary embolism with shock needs reperfusion.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Reperfuse the lung.

front: COPD and a resting saturation of 86 percent.
bottom: Oxygen is indicated at or below 88 percent.

bullets.clue: 90 percent is not the qualifying number.
bullets.treat: Prescribe oxygen, then the inhalers.
bullets.trap: Do not withhold oxygen because the patient quit.

source.recommendation: Long-term oxygen is for resting saturation at or below 88 percent.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Oxygen is indicated at or below 88 percent.

front: Asthma symptoms most days. The only inhaler is a rescue drug.

bullets.clue: A long-acting beta agonist alone is unsafe.
bullets.treat: Start an inhaled corticosteroid.
bullets.trap: Do not refill the rescue inhaler alone.

source.recommendation: Frequent rescue use means an inhaled corticosteroid is required.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Add an inhaled steroid.

front: Pneumonia and a large pleural fluid that looks like pus.

bullets.clue: A small free fluid can be watched.
bullets.treat: Tap, then drain a complicated fluid.
bullets.trap: Do not leave pus on antibiotics alone.

source.recommendation: Empyema and complicated parapneumonic effusions are drained.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Drain pus.

front: A healthy adult has outpatient pneumonia and no other disease.

bullets.clue: Comorbidities change the regimen.
bullets.treat: Use the healthy-adult regimen.
bullets.trap: Do not start a fluoroquinolone first.

source.recommendation: Healthy outpatients do not start with a fluoroquinolone.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Amoxicillin, doxycycline, or a macrolide.

front: Fever, stiff neck, and a planned lumbar puncture in an hour.

bullets.clue: The puncture must not delay the drug.
bullets.treat: Drug first, then the puncture.
bullets.trap: Do not wait for the procedure.

source.recommendation: Empiric antibiotics for suspected meningitis are immediate. The 2004 principles still govern the delay rule.

diagram.alt: Numbered steps. Antibiotics now.

front: Who needs ampicillin added for meningitis?

bullets.clue: The extra organism is Listeria.
bullets.treat: Add ampicillin to vancomycin and a cephalosporin.
bullets.trap: Do not use two drugs for every adult.

front: A new HIV diagnosis. The CD4 count is not back.

bullets.clue: The count does not gate treatment.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Start treatment now.

front: An HIV-negative partner of a person with HIV wants prevention.

bullets.trap: Do not use prevention drugs to treat HIV.

bullets.trap: Do not use one drug.

bullets.trap: Do not start a fluoroquinolone.

front: Drug-susceptible active tuberculosis.

bullets.trap: Do not ignore a very high viral load.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Treat immune-active disease.

front: Chronic hepatitis C and no symptoms.

bullets.clue: Symptoms are not the indication.

bullets.trap: Do not wait for cirrhosis.

source.recommendation: Nearly all chronic hepatitis C is treated.

front: The serum-ascites albumin gradient is 1.4.

bullets.clue: 1.1 or higher is portal. Under 1.1 is peritoneal.

bullets.trap: Do not start tuberculosis drugs for a high gradient.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Portal hypertension.

front: A variceal bleed has stopped. The patient is stable.

front: New iron deficiency at age 55.

bullets.trap: Do not recheck the blood count and stop.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Colonoscopy, not iron alone.

front: Burning epigastric pain. Age 32. No alarm symptom.

bottom: Do not give an antimotility drug.

bullets.trap: Do not use loperamide alone.

front: Last known well was 2 hours ago. CT shows no blood. The deficit is disabling.

front: Brief electric face pain when chewing. The exam is normal.

bullets.trap: Do not start an opioid.

diagram.alt: Do and do not. Carbamazepine.
